# Dynamic changes and relationships among AI Literacy, job crafting, and career growth in new nurses in the AI era: A multicenter three-wave 

# longitudinal study

## ARTICLE INFO ABSTRACT

### _Keywords:_ _Background:_ Artificial intelligence (AI) technologies are being rapidly integrated into the nursing field. As a new 

AI literacy and emerging force within the nursing workforce, new nurses face both opportunities and challenges in their Job crafting career growth in the AI era. AI literacy has become increasingly important and may play a critical role in shaping Career growth

the career growth of new nurses. However, research examining the dynamic changes, influencing factors, and 

New nurse underlying mechanisms of career growth among new nurses in the context of AI remains limited.

### _Objective:_ To explore the dynamic trajectories of AI literacy, job crafting, and career growth among new nurses, 

and to examine the longitudinal mediating role of job crafting in the relationship between AI literacy and career 

growth.

### _Design:_ A multicenter, three-wave longitudinal study.

### _Methods:_ The AI Literacy Scale, Job Crafting Scale, and Career Growth Scale were administered in April 2025 

(T1), July 2025 (T2), and October 2025 (T3) to 339 new nurses from five tertiary general hospitals across different regions of China. SPSS 26.0 and AMOS 26.0 were used to construct longitudinal mediation models and 

conduct data analyses.

### _Results:_ Across T1, T2, and T3, the mean scores of AI literacy and career growth showed a pattern of initial 

decline followed by an increase over time, whereas the mean score of job crafting demonstrated a continuous upward trend. At all time points, AI literacy, job crafting, and career growth were significantly and positively correlated. AI literacy positively predicted career growth in new nurses, and job crafting played a significant 

longitudinal mediating role in this relationship.

### _Conclusions:_ AI literacy among new nurses can predict their future career growth through the mediating role of 

job crafting. Hospitals and nursing educators should attach importance to AI-related training and guidance for new nurses and strive to create organizational environments characterized by appropriate autonomy and sup- port. Encouraging reasonable job crafting is crucial for fostering career growth among new nurses in the AI era 

and for promoting the sustainable development of the nursing profession.

Due to limited clinical experience, high role adaptation pressure, and an as-yet-unsettled pro- fessional identity, new nurses are more likely to experience career confusion and developmental uncertainty when confronted with high- intensity work environments, complex interpersonal relationships, and rapidly evolving medical technologies (Meng et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2025c; Zheng et al., 2023). According to a report by NSI (Solutions, 2024), approximately 23.8% of new nurses left their jobs within the first year of employment in 2023, and career growth has been identified as one of the primary factors influencing turnover intention (Martini et al., 2025). Therefore, the career growth of new nurses not only af- fects their individual competence but also directly impacts the stability of the nursing workforce and the quality of healthcare services, making it a critical issue that urgently requires attention in nursing management and nursing education.

## 2. Background

Career growth refers to the continuous improvement individuals achieve in professional competence, career goals, psychological matu- rity, and developmental potential through learning and practice over the course of their career development (Weng et al., 2010). For nurses, career growth is reflected not only in the accumulation of clinical skills and professional knowledge but also in enhanced occupational value and confidence in future development (Liu et al., 2015). This is partic- ularly important for new nurses at the early stage of their careers, as it is key to fully leveraging their strengths and enhancing their professional competitiveness (Ni et al., 2025). Positive career growth helps new nurses adapt more quickly to the clinical environment, reduces turnover rates, and promotes long-term career well-being, ultimately improving the quality of patient care (Kato et al., 2025). With the advent of the artificial intelligence (AI) era, nursing work models, service processes, and professional competency structures are undergoing profound changes. Consequently, the career growth of new nurses is inevitably influenced by AI technologies. Failure to adapt smoothly to this new environment may expose them to various challenges and uncertainties ([El-Bassal et al., 2025;](#analysis-guangli-lu-software-project-administration-methodology-aydogan-s-kok-ay-ergezen-fd-bozkurt-sa-2026-the-effect-of-role-playing-and-zhengyi-ma-investigation-formal-analysis-data-curation-juntong-ai-based-learning-on-nursing-students-knowledge-of-the-nursing-process-and) Michalowski et al., 2026). However, existing studies have primarily examined nurses' career growth from traditional perspectives such as individual, organizational, and social factors, while paying insufficient attention to the influence of technological trans- formations such as AI. Therefore, it is necessary to re-examine the mechanisms influencing the career growth of new nurses within the context of technological change. Doing so will help reveal new charac- teristics of nursing talent development and provide a theoretical basis for optimizing training and management models for new nurses, thereby promoting the sustainable development of the nursing profession. As AI technologies rapidly penetrate the nursing field, AI literacy may gradually become a key factor influencing the career growth of new nurses (Hoelscher and Pugh, 2025). AI literacy is defined as an in- dividual's comprehensive ability to effectively understand, evaluate, apply, and manage AI technologies in intelligent contexts (Wang et al., 2023). According to the Technology Acceptance Model, individuals' perceptions of the “usefulness” and “ease of use” of AI influence their attitudes toward the technology (Venkatesh and Davis, 2000). Building on this model, Ho and Le further incorporated AI literacy, suggesting that it serves as a key antecedent influencing individuals' perceived usefulness of AI and their attitudes toward its use ([Ho and Le, 2026)](#analysis-guangli-lu-software-project-administration-methodology-aydogan-s-kok-ay-ergezen-fd-bozkurt-sa-2026-the-effect-of-role-playing-and-zhengyi-ma-investigation-formal-analysis-data-curation-juntong-ai-based-learning-on-nursing-students-knowledge-of-the-nursing-process-and). In nursing practice, only when nurses possess a certain level of AI literacy and subjectively recognize the value of AI are they more likely to actively engage with it and apply it to improve the quality of care and patient safety ([Cho and Seo, 2024;](#analysis-guangli-lu-software-project-administration-methodology-aydogan-s-kok-ay-ergezen-fd-bozkurt-sa-2026-the-effect-of-role-playing-and-zhengyi-ma-investigation-formal-analysis-data-curation-juntong-ai-based-learning-on-nursing-students-knowledge-of-the-nursing-process-and) [Chu et al., 2026)](#analysis-guangli-lu-software-project-administration-methodology-aydogan-s-kok-ay-ergezen-fd-bozkurt-sa-2026-the-effect-of-role-playing-and-zhengyi-ma-investigation-formal-analysis-data-curation-juntong-ai-based-learning-on-nursing-students-knowledge-of-the-nursing-process-and). For nurses, AI lit- eracy differs from mere technical competence or digital literacy. Tech- nical competence primarily refers to proficiency in operating specific tools or systems, with its core focus on whether one can use technology effectively. Digital literacy, in contrast, emphasizes general abilities 

such as accessing, evaluating, and using information, with the core focus on whether one can effectively process and utilize information. Building upon both, AI literacy further extends these capabilities. It not only in- volves a critical understanding of the fundamental principles, technical functions, and ethical risks of artificial intelligence, but also encom- passes the practical ability to judge, interpret, and calibrate AI outputs in specific clinical contexts, as well as to responsibly and appropriately integrate AI tools into nursing workflows ([Chung et al., 2025;](#analysis-guangli-lu-software-project-administration-methodology-aydogan-s-kok-ay-ergezen-fd-bozkurt-sa-2026-the-effect-of-role-playing-and-zhengyi-ma-investigation-formal-analysis-data-curation-juntong-ai-based-learning-on-nursing-students-knowledge-of-the-nursing-process-and) Hoelscher and Pugh, 2025). According to the Nursing AI Literacy and Governance Framework (NAIL-G), AI literacy expands the boundaries of both tech- nical skills and digital literacy. Nurses are positioned not merely as users of technology, but as interpreters of AI-generated outputs and bearers of responsibility. When necessary, they are expected to correct or even reject AI recommendations, thereby ensuring patient safety and equity (Ibrahim et al., 2026). Therefore, AI literacy, as a comprehensive com- petency, is fundamentally distinct from general technical skills. It aligns more closely with the core mechanism of career growth among new nurses and determines their capacity for continuous learning, profes- sional judgment, and safe and appropriate use of AI in clinical decision- making. As such, it has strong practical implications and significantly influences job crafting and overall career growth (Liu et al., 2025b, 2025c; Simms, 2025). As a new force within nursing teams, new nurses may have certain advantages in accepting and learning new technolo- gies, potentially exhibiting more open attitudes toward AI. This posi- tions them with substantial potential for developing AI literacy and integrating it deeply into nursing practice ([El-Sayed et al., 2025;](#analysis-guangli-lu-software-project-administration-methodology-aydogan-s-kok-ay-ergezen-fd-bozkurt-sa-2026-the-effect-of-role-playing-and-zhengyi-ma-investigation-formal-analysis-data-curation-juntong-ai-based-learning-on-nursing-students-knowledge-of-the-nursing-process-and) Subasi et al., 2025).

Based on the Job Demands–Resources (JD-R) model, AI literacy can be regarded as a novel form of job resource ([Arboh et al., 2025)](#analysis-guangli-lu-software-project-administration-methodology-aydogan-s-kok-ay-ergezen-fd-bozkurt-sa-2026-the-effect-of-role-playing-and-zhengyi-ma-investigation-formal-analysis-data-curation-juntong-ai-based-learning-on-nursing-students-knowledge-of-the-nursing-process-and). Unlike traditional job resources, AI literacy is not only reflected in technical usage but is also influenced by the complexity of the technology and the awareness of ethical risks ([El Arab et al., 2025)](#analysis-guangli-lu-software-project-administration-methodology-aydogan-s-kok-ay-ergezen-fd-bozkurt-sa-2026-the-effect-of-role-playing-and-zhengyi-ma-investigation-formal-analysis-data-curation-juntong-ai-based-learning-on-nursing-students-knowledge-of-the-nursing-process-and). Nurses' AI literacy may evolve dynamically through interactions with AI, shaped by accumu- lated clinical experience, feedback from technology use, and real-world ethical considerations ([El Arab et al., 2025;](#analysis-guangli-lu-software-project-administration-methodology-aydogan-s-kok-ay-ergezen-fd-bozkurt-sa-2026-the-effect-of-role-playing-and-zhengyi-ma-investigation-formal-analysis-data-curation-juntong-ai-based-learning-on-nursing-students-knowledge-of-the-nursing-process-and) Kelly et al., 2023). Although existing studies have rarely directly examined the relationship between AI literacy and career growth, some recent research has explored the value of AI in nursing from an applied perspective. For example, studies have shown that AI-based decision support systems can identify adverse events at an earlier stage and streamline nursing workflows ([Awad et al., 2025)](#analysis-guangli-lu-software-project-administration-methodology-aydogan-s-kok-ay-ergezen-fd-bozkurt-sa-2026-the-effect-of-role-playing-and-zhengyi-ma-investigation-formal-analysis-data-curation-juntong-ai-based-learning-on-nursing-students-knowledge-of-the-nursing-process-and). AI-driven triage models can optimize resource allocation, thereby improving triage efficiency and patient outcomes ([El Arab and Al Moosa, 2025)](#analysis-guangli-lu-software-project-administration-methodology-aydogan-s-kok-ay-ergezen-fd-bozkurt-sa-2026-the-effect-of-role-playing-and-zhengyi-ma-investigation-formal-analysis-data-curation-juntong-ai-based-learning-on-nursing-students-knowledge-of-the-nursing-process-and). In addition, nurse-led AI-assisted perioperative health education can enhance patients' coping strategies and psycho- logical well-being (Shen et al., 2025). In the field of nursing education, generative AI is being explored for applications such as generating teaching cases and simulating patient interactions. AI-assisted nursing procedure training allows nursing students to refine their clinical reasoning through iterative trial and error, while also improving empathy, learning satisfaction, self-directed learning ability, and clin- ical competence ([Arkan et al., 2025;](#analysis-guangli-lu-software-project-administration-methodology-aydogan-s-kok-ay-ergezen-fd-bozkurt-sa-2026-the-effect-of-role-playing-and-zhengyi-ma-investigation-formal-analysis-data-curation-juntong-ai-based-learning-on-nursing-students-knowledge-of-the-nursing-process-and) Jeon and Jeong, 2026). Moreover, the experiences of nursing educators and students with AI have become key indicators for evaluating its integration into education. As a collaborator in instructional design, AI can to some extent relieve edu- cators from repetitive tasks, enabling them to focus more on higher-level teaching activities ([Ali and Shaban, 2026a, 2026b)](#analysis-guangli-lu-software-project-administration-methodology-aydogan-s-kok-ay-ergezen-fd-bozkurt-sa-2026-the-effect-of-role-playing-and-zhengyi-ma-investigation-formal-analysis-data-curation-juntong-ai-based-learning-on-nursing-students-knowledge-of-the-nursing-process-and). Nursing students generally hold more open attitudes toward AI; however, while some are able to critically evaluate AI-generated content, others tend to over-rely on it, highlighting the need for systematic development of AI literacy ([Ali and Shaban, 2026a, 2026b)](#analysis-guangli-lu-software-project-administration-methodology-aydogan-s-kok-ay-ergezen-fd-bozkurt-sa-2026-the-effect-of-role-playing-and-zhengyi-ma-investigation-formal-analysis-data-curation-juntong-ai-based-learning-on-nursing-students-knowledge-of-the-nursing-process-and). Therefore, AI literacy should be considered a crucial component of nursing education. When new nurses possess a higher level of AI literacy, their understanding, acceptance, and application of AI technologies are correspondingly enhanced (Sürme et al., 2026). This not only enables them to more efficiently acquire and integrate clinical information and optimize nursing decision-making processes, but also fosters creative thinking and self-

T1 phase: In April 2025 (T1), a baseline offline survey was conducted using the hospital human resources system. Each participant was assigned a unique anonymous identification number (ID), which was retained in T2 and T3 to ensure rigor and traceability. A total of 400 questionnaires were distributed; after excluding 19 invalid re- sponses, 381 valid questionnaires were obtained, yielding an effec- tive response rate of 95.25%.

T2 phase: Three months after T1 (July 2025, T2), a second round of surveys was conducted among the new nurses who had completed the valid T1 survey. A total of 381 questionnaires were distributed; 24 participants were lost to follow-up, resulting in 357 valid re- sponses and an effective response rate of 93.70%.

T3 phase: Three months after T2 (October 2025, T3), a third round of follow-up surveys was conducted among participants who had completed the valid T2 survey. A total of 357 questionnaires were distributed; 18 participants were lost to follow-up, resulting in 339 valid responses and an effective response rate of 94.96%.

Through this three-wave tracking design, a total of 339 new nurses completed all rounds of the survey, yielding an overall effective response rate of 84.75%.

### _3.4._ _Instruments_

#### _3.4.1._ _Demographic characteristics questionnaire_

Based on the objectives of this study, a demographic characteristics questionnaire for new nurses was developed by the researchers. The questionnaire collected information on gender, educational level, only- child status, marital status, employment and personnel relationship, reasons for choosing nursing as a career, and average monthly income.

#### _3.4.2._ _AI literacy scale_

AI literacy was assessed using the AI Literacy Scale developed by Wang et al. (2023). The scale comprises 12 items across four dimensions: awareness, use, evaluation, and ethics. Responses are rated on a 7-point Likert scale ranging from 1 (“strongly disagree”) to 7 (“strongly agree”), with higher scores indicating higher levels of AI literacy. Previous research by Liu et al. (2025b, 2025c) has demonstrated good applica- bility of this scale in the Chinese nursing context. In the present study, the Cronbach's α coefficients of the scale were 0.943 at T1, 0.936 at T2, and 0.875 at T3.

#### _3.4.3._ _Job crafting scale_

Job crafting was measured using the Job Crafting Scale developed by Tims et al. (2012) and translated into Chinese by Liao (2013). The scale includes 21 items across four dimensions: increasing structural job re- sources, increasing social job resources, increasing challenging job de- mands, and decreasing hindering job demands. Items are rated on a 5- point Likert scale ranging from 1 (“completely disagree”) to 5 (“completely agree”), with higher scores indicating higher levels of job crafting. The applicability of this scale among Chinese nurses has been validated by Wen and Wang (2025). In this study, the Cronbach's α coefficients were 0.940 at T1, 0.943 at T2, and 0.922 at T3.

#### _3.4.4._ _Career growth scale_

Career growth was assessed using the Nurse Career Growth Scale developed by Ni et al. (2023). The scale consists of 17 items across three dimensions: professional ability and attribute improvement, career promotion and prestige increase, and career goal progress. Responses are rated on a 5-point Likert scale ranging from 1 (“completely disagree”) to 5 (“completely agree”), with higher scores indicating faster career growth. The scale has demonstrated good reliability and validity among Chinese nurses (Ni et al., 2025). In the current study, the Cron- bach's α coefficients were 0.919 at T1, 0.928 at T2, and 0.919 at T3.

### _3.5._ _Statistical analysis_

Data analysis in this study was conducted using SPSS and AMOS. First, Harman's single-factor test was applied to assess common method bias. Second, descriptive statistics were performed to summarize the demographic characteristics of participants who completed all three waves, and their baseline data were compared with those who did not complete all waves. Next, confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) was con- ducted for each scale at different time points, followed by tests of lon- gitudinal measurement invariance across time. In addition, the correlations and dynamic changes of the study variables across T1, T2, and T3 were analyzed. On this basis, a three-wave longitudinal media- tion model was constructed and analyzed using AMOS 26.0, and com- parisons were made with alternative models. Finally, the mediating effects and their 95% confidence intervals (CI) were examined using the Bootstrapping method with 5000 resamples, along with a sensitivity analysis. A _p_-value of less than 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

### _3.6._ _Ethical considerations_

This study did not involve unethical behavior or human clinical ex- periments and did not cause physical or psychological harm to partici- pants. Ethical issues were given high priority. Prior to questionnaire distribution, approval was obtained from the hospitals and nursing de- partments involved. Participants were fully informed of the study pur- pose and significance, and written informed consent was obtained from all participants, who participated voluntarily. The survey was conducted anonymously, and participants were assured that their responses would be used solely for research purposes and that they could withdraw at any time. These measures ensured the protection of participants' privacy and data confidentiality. This study was reviewed and approved by Biomedical Research Ethics Committee of Henan University (approval number: HUSOM2025-1017; approval date: January 21, 2025).

## 4. Results

### _4.1._ _Common method bias tests_

Harman's single-factor test was conducted to examine potential common method bias. The results showed that the first factor accounted for 33.775%, 33.077%, and 29.314% of the total variance at T1, T2, and T3, respectively, all of which were below the 40% threshold. These findings indicate that common method bias was not a serious concern in this study.

### _4.2._ _Participants' demographic characteristics_

Among the 339 new nurses who completed all three waves of the survey, 23.89% were male and 76.11% were female. A total of 77.29% held a bachelor's degree, and 57.23% were not only children. Most participants were unmarried (94.10%). In terms of employment status, 59.59% were contract-based staff. More than half of the new nurses chose nursing voluntarily (65.19%). In addition, the majority reported a monthly income of less than 8000 RMB (88.49%).

In addition, baseline demographic characteristics, as well as scores of AI literacy, job crafting, and career growth, were compared between participants who completed all three waves and those who completed only the baseline survey but missed at least one subsequent wave. The results showed no significant systematic differences between the two groups (all _p \>_ 0.05), indicating good sample stability and supporting the suitability for subsequent longitudinal analyses. ### _4.3._ _Stability of the longitudinal measurement structure_

To examine the stability of the measurement structure of all scales across time, this study first conducted preliminary confirmatory factor analyses (CFA) for all scales at three time points (T1, T2, and T3), fol- lowed by tests of longitudinal measurement invariance. The CFA results for each time point are presented in [Table 2.](#43-stability-of-the-longitudinal-measurement-structure) The model fit indices for the AI literacy scale and the career growth scale were within acceptable ranges at all time points (Kenny et al., 2015). The model fit indices of the job crafting scale at Time 1 were suboptimal. Item-level diagnostic re- sults indicated that no single item was primarily responsible for the poor model fit (see Supplementary material 1). This may be related to new nurses' insufficient understanding of job crafting at an early stage. However, the GFI and AGFI indices still reached relatively high levels. Moreover, the model fit improved at both Time 2 and Time 3. Therefore, the scale demonstrated an acceptable measurement structure across all time points (Shi et al., 2019).

In addition, given the relatively low degrees of freedom of the models at single time points and the tendency for RMSEA to be inflated in low-

### _4.5._ _Mediation effect analysis_

In this study, AI literacy measured at T1, T2, and T3 was treated as the independent variable, job crafting as the mediating variable, and career growth as the dependent variable to construct a three-wave longitudinal mediation model. Based on the inclusion of autore- gressive paths of each variable across the three measurements, the model examined the predictive effects of AI literacy at earlier time points on subsequent job crafting and career growth, as well as the predictive effect of earlier job crafting on subsequent career growth (see Fig. 1).

This study further constructed two alternative models for compari- son with the original model. In the reverse mediation model, the di- rection of the mediating pathway was reversed and specified as career growth → job crafting → AI literacy. The direct effect only model retained only the autoregressive paths and direct effect paths. As shown in Table 6, the original model demonstrated an acceptable model fit based on multiple fit indices and performed better than both the reverse mediation model and the direct effect only model (Hu and Bentler, 1999). significant (_p \<_ 0.001), demonstrating good temporal stability. Regarding cross-lagged effects, in the T1 → T2 interval, T1 AI literacy significantly and positively predicted subsequent T2 job crafting (β = 0.466, p _\<_ 0.001) and T2 career growth (β = 0.272, p _\<_ 0.001), while T1 job crafting significantly and positively predicted subsequent T2 career growth (β = 0.262, p _\<_ 0.001). In the T2 → T3 interval, T2 AI literacy significantly and positively predicted subsequent T3 job crafting (β = 0.332, p _\<_ 0.001) and T3 career growth (β = 0.235, p _\<_ 0.001), and T2 job crafting significantly and positively predicted subsequent T3 career growth (β = 0.225, p _\<_ 0.001). In addition, in the T1 → T3 interval, T1 AI literacy also directly and significantly predicted subsequent T3 career growth (β = 0.154, p _\<_ 0.001).

Furthermore, the Bootstrapping method with 5000 resamples was applied to further examine the cross-temporal effect of T1 AI literacy on T3 career growth through T2 job crafting, thereby ensuring the temporal sequencing required for longitudinal mediation analysis. As shown in Table 7, the total effect of T1 AIL on T3 CG was 0.259 (p _\<_ 0.001, 95% CI: 0.169, 0.351). The direct effect of the path “T1 AIL → T3 CG” was 0.154 (p _\<_ 0.001, 95% CI: 0.067, 0.244), accounting for 59.46% of the total effect. The indirect effect through job crafting (“T1 AIL → T2 JC → T3 CG”) was 0.105 (p _\<_ 0.001, 95% CI: 0.072, 0.143), accounting for 40.54% of the total effect. These findings support Hypotheses 4 and 5.

### _4.6._ _Sensitivity analysis_

To further examine the robustness of the longitudinal mediation model, this study included educational level as a covariate in the model for sensitivity analysis (see Supplementary material 2). The results showed that, after controlling for educational level, the direction of the main pathways remained consistent with the original model. Following bootstrapping tests, both the direct effect (Effect = 0.139, _P \<_ 0.001, 95% CI: 0.047, 0.232) and the indirect effect (Effect = 0.114, P _\<_ 0.001, 95% CI: 0.080, 0.153) remained statistically significant, confirming the robustness of the findings.

## 5. Discussion

### _5.1._ _Dynamic changes in study variables_

Based on the three-wave follow-up measurements, the mean level of AI literacy among new nurses exhibited a pattern of initial decline fol- lowed by an increase over time. This finding suggests that AI literacy among new nurses does not develop in a linear manner, but instead undergoes a dynamic process during the early stages of their careers. This pattern can be further understood through the Technology Accep- tance Model, which posits that individuals' cognition and behavior in the

early stages of adopting new technologies are often influenced by their perceived “usefulness” and “ease of use.” As practical experience accu- mulates, these perceptions may change (Venkatesh and Davis, 2000). Currently, new nurses are typically exposed to AI-related knowledge and education during their nursing training, providing them with a certain theoretical foundation and relatively positive expectations toward AI technologies. However, in real clinical practice, the combined effects of early career stress and excessive transitional shock may lead to a tem- porary decline in new nurses' AI literacy. During the transition from novice nurses to clinical practitioners, they often experience transitional shock. Due to an initially unstable state of professional adaptation, although they may possess a certain level of theoretical knowledge of AI, they often struggle to translate it into practical clinical competence (Liu et al., 2024a). In addition, the complexity of clinical environments and technical workflows, together with high workload and professional re- sponsibility pressure, further challenge their effective application of AI technologies ([Aydogan et al., 2026;](#analysis-guangli-lu-software-project-administration-methodology-aydogan-s-kok-ay-ergezen-fd-bozkurt-sa-2026-the-effect-of-role-playing-and-zhengyi-ma-investigation-formal-analysis-data-curation-juntong-ai-based-learning-on-nursing-students-knowledge-of-the-nursing-process-and) [El Arab et al., 2025)](#analysis-guangli-lu-software-project-administration-methodology-aydogan-s-kok-ay-ergezen-fd-bozkurt-sa-2026-the-effect-of-role-playing-and-zhengyi-ma-investigation-formal-analysis-data-curation-juntong-ai-based-learning-on-nursing-students-knowledge-of-the-nursing-process-and). However, with 

the accumulation of clinical experience, new nurses' understanding of AI technology may gradually shift from abstract cognition to concrete experiential knowledge, while their ethical awareness, critical thinking, and ability to interpret and apply technology are also enhanced (Jing 

literacy depend not only on theoretical education but also require tar- geted training and guidance within clinical practice to accelerate the translation of knowledge into clinical competence.

The results also showed a continuous upward trend in the mean level of job crafting among new nurses, reflecting a gradual process of pro- actively adjusting work approaches. Previous studies have demonstrated that nurses' job crafting is influenced by work experience, which further 

rely more on established procedures and instructions from supervisors, leaving limited room for proactively adjusting tasks and relationships ([Felder et al., 2024;](#analysis-guangli-lu-software-project-administration-methodology-aydogan-s-kok-ay-ergezen-fd-bozkurt-sa-2026-the-effect-of-role-playing-and-zhengyi-ma-investigation-formal-analysis-data-curation-juntong-ai-based-learning-on-nursing-students-knowledge-of-the-nursing-process-and) Liu et al., 2025d). However, as familiarity with institutional systems and workflows increases and professional compe- tence improves, new nurses gradually gain a greater sense of control over their work context. Their motivation to buffer work stress and enhance work meaning through task crafting, relational crafting, and cognitive crafting continues to grow. Within existing frameworks, they become increasingly capable of improving person–job fit by fine-tuning task execution, actively seeking support, and reconstructing the mean- ing of work, thereby promoting job crafting behaviors (Long et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2025a). Accordingly, we suggest that organizations should actively guide job crafting among new nurses by providing moderate autonomy and a supportive environment early in their careers, encouraging them to achieve both personal development and organi- zational goals through proactive job crafting.

In addition, the mean level of career growth among new nurses also followed a pattern of initial decline followed by an increase, indicating fluctuations in career adaptation during the career growth process. This finding aligns with the “adaptation curve” proposed in role adaptation

theory ([Dukerich, 2001)](#analysis-guangli-lu-software-project-administration-methodology-aydogan-s-kok-ay-ergezen-fd-bozkurt-sa-2026-the-effect-of-role-playing-and-zhengyi-ma-investigation-formal-analysis-data-curation-juntong-ai-based-learning-on-nursing-students-knowledge-of-the-nursing-process-and). New nurses may initially hold high profes- sional expectations and a strong sense of career development aspiration toward the nursing profession, with considerable confidence in their future development prospects ([Han et al., 2024)](#analysis-guangli-lu-software-project-administration-methodology-aydogan-s-kok-ay-ergezen-fd-bozkurt-sa-2026-the-effect-of-role-playing-and-zhengyi-ma-investigation-formal-analysis-data-curation-juntong-ai-based-learning-on-nursing-students-knowledge-of-the-nursing-process-and). However, upon entering a high-intensity and fast-paced clinical environment, early career challenges such as heavy workload and complex interpersonal relationships become apparent. New nurses therefore begin to experi- ence transitional shock, which may weaken their confidence in and evaluation of career growth (Liu et al., 2025d; Zheng et al., 2025). With the accumulation of working time and clinical experience, new nurses gradually complete the adaptation from a “transition phase” to a “development phase” of their professional role. At the same time, organizational support increasingly takes effect, helping them recon- struct a more positive perception of their own development (Liu et al., 2024a, 2024b; Qiu et al., 2025). This result further underscores that new nurses' career growth may involve a process moving from an idealistic phase to a reality-shock phase and then to an improvement phase. Hospitals should therefore provide systematic training programs, continuous feedback, and sustained support to facilitate the long-term career growth of new nurses.

### _5.2._ _Direct effects of AI literacy on career growth in new nurses_

To the best of our knowledge, this study is the first to use a longi- tudinal design to confirm that AI literacy directly and positively predicts subsequent career growth in new nurses. Previous studies have pri- marily focused on the status of nurses' information literacy or attitudes toward AI and their effects on work attitudes and competencies. For example, one study reported that information literacy and nursing informatics competencies influenced nurses' attitudes toward evidence- based practice (Mudallal et al., 2025). Other studies have shown that attitudes toward AI are important predictors of nurses' creative self- efficacy and clinical reasoning ability ([Atalla et al., 2025)](#analysis-guangli-lu-software-project-administration-methodology-aydogan-s-kok-ay-ergezen-fd-bozkurt-sa-2026-the-effect-of-role-playing-and-zhengyi-ma-investigation-formal-analysis-data-curation-juntong-ai-based-learning-on-nursing-students-knowledge-of-the-nursing-process-and). In addition, some studies on nursing students indicate that there remains a need to promote AI-related education and training, so as to enhance their AI literacy and alleviate AI anxiety, thereby enabling them to possess AI self-efficacy in nursing practice ([Al-Olaimat et al., 2025;](#analysis-guangli-lu-software-project-administration-methodology-aydogan-s-kok-ay-ergezen-fd-bozkurt-sa-2026-the-effect-of-role-playing-and-zhengyi-ma-investigation-formal-analysis-data-curation-juntong-ai-based-learning-on-nursing-students-knowledge-of-the-nursing-process-and) [Berdida et al., 2026;](#analysis-guangli-lu-software-project-administration-methodology-aydogan-s-kok-ay-ergezen-fd-bozkurt-sa-2026-the-effect-of-role-playing-and-zhengyi-ma-investigation-formal-analysis-data-curation-juntong-ai-based-learning-on-nursing-students-knowledge-of-the-nursing-process-and) LaGore et al., 2025). Therefore, AI literacy education should be regarded as a continuous process that extends from formal schooling to onboarding training. Higher AI literacy indicates stronger technological understanding, data awareness, and problem-solving abilities, enabling new nurses to more quickly master the operational logic of intelligent systems and effectively integrate them into clinical practice (Hoelscher and Pugh, 2025). When new nurses are able to accept and skillfully use AI tools to improve work efficiency, reduce cognitive load, and enhance the quality of nursing decision-making, they are more likely to perceive personal value and growth opportunities in intelligent nursing contexts, viewing technological change as an opportunity rather than a threat to their development ([Fang et al., 2025;](#analysis-guangli-lu-software-project-administration-methodology-aydogan-s-kok-ay-ergezen-fd-bozkurt-sa-2026-the-effect-of-role-playing-and-zhengyi-ma-investigation-formal-analysis-data-curation-juntong-ai-based-learning-on-nursing-students-knowledge-of-the-nursing-process-and) Liu et al., 2025b, 2025c; S¸ims¸ek et al., 2025). This positive process of career competence adap- tation helps new nurses form a clear understanding of their develop- mental pathways, thereby providing a solid foundation for career growth (Walden et al., 2022). Given that career growth influences both long-term retention and the quality of nursing practice, nursing man- agement departments should attach great importance to cultivating AI literacy as a key driver of career growth among new nurses.

### _5.3._ _The longitudinal mediating role of job crafting_

Furthermore, the results demonstrated that job crafting played a significant longitudinal mediating role in the relationship between AI literacy and career growth in new nurses. Specifically, AI literacy among new nurses is longitudinally associated with the development of job crafting, which in turn predicts their subsequent career growth. Previous research has shown that acceptance of AI can dynamically influence nurses' job crafting, supporting our findings (Jing et al., 2026a, 2026b). 

As an important prerequisite for AI acceptance, AI literacy is not only a critical competency for new nurses entering clinical practice but also gradually transforms into positive attitudes toward AI use over time, thereby promoting job crafting and subsequently influencing long-term career development (Liu et al., 2025b, 2025c; Schiavo et al., 2024). AI literacy serves as a key resource enabling new nurses to enhance work efficiency and personal competence through intelligent tools (Mayer et al., 2025). Confidence in using AI technologies stimulates their intention to proactively reshape job content and optimize workflows, empowering them to improve efficiency, reduce repetitive tasks, enhance autonomy and creativity, flexibly adjust care plans according to patients' needs, and improve work quality. Through these processes, new nurses gradually achieve self-directed work goal attainment and advance their career growth ([Chen, 2024;](#analysis-guangli-lu-software-project-administration-methodology-aydogan-s-kok-ay-ergezen-fd-bozkurt-sa-2026-the-effect-of-role-playing-and-zhengyi-ma-investigation-formal-analysis-data-curation-juntong-ai-based-learning-on-nursing-students-knowledge-of-the-nursing-process-and) Miao et al., 2023). Accord- ingly, job crafting represents a dynamic process that accumulates over time (Liaquat et al., 2025). As new nurses increasingly engage in job crafting, their potential for career growth is gradually unlocked, and this effect persists over time, suggesting that job crafting may constitute a deeper psychological and behavioral mechanism linking AI literacy and career growth in new nurses.

### _5.4._ _Implications for education and practice_

These findings have important implications for nursing education and practice. First, nursing educators should fully recognize that AI literacy has gradually become a critical component of new nurses' pro- fessional competence in the current era, and should incorporate AI lit- eracy as a core competency into pre-service education and training programs. In terms of training design, it is recommended that nursing educators develop a tiered and progressive AI literacy training frame- work to support the transition from foundational understanding to clinical application (Hoelscher and Pugh, 2025; Ibrahim et al., 2026). The first stage is a “basic AI cognition module,” which introduces the functions and applications of AI through expert lectures and online courses, helping new nurses understand the fundamental principles, advantages, and limitations of AI and establish a solid cognitive foun- dation. The second stage is an “AI operation and interpretation module,” which focuses on skill development, enabling new nurses to use AI systems appropriately and accurately interpret AI-generated outputs. For example, through training with clinical decision support systems, they learn how to read AI recommendations, understand their under- lying rationale, and evaluate their applicability in relation to patient conditions. The third stage is a “human–machine collaboration module,” which aims to develop decision-making abilities in complex clinical contexts. Simulation-based learning can be used to construct dynamic and complex clinical cases, requiring new nurses to analyze situations where AI recommendations conflict with their own clinical judgment and thereby cultivate critical thinking skills. The fourth stage is an “AI ethics and safety module,” which strengthens risk awareness and pro- fessional responsibility. This module addresses issues such as data pri- vacy, safety, trust, accountability, and informed patient consent through ethical dilemma discussions. For instance, scenarios involving AI algo- rithmic bias can be used to train new nurses to identify potential risks, raise questions, and revise nursing plans accordingly. In implementa- tion, these training modules should not be delivered in isolation but should be integrated into existing courses such as nursing informatics, evidence-based nursing practice, and clinical internships. By combining AI literacy with professional knowledge, this approach facilitates the transformation of competence into clinical practice and ultimately supports new nurses' career growth (Ibrahim et al., 2026; Xie et al., 2026).

Second, as hospitals introduce information systems and intelligent devices, they should provide new nurses with progressive learning support and practical opportunities. It is important to note that the extent to which AI technologies are integrated into clinical workflows may vary significantly depending on hospital infrastructure, 

departmental functions, and patient characteristics. In some tertiary general hospitals, nurses have access to a wide range of AI systems and digital tools, such as AI-based clinical decision support systems, early warning and risk assessment systems, electronic documentation and quality control platforms, wearable devices for vital sign monitoring and anomaly detection, intelligent infusion monitoring systems, fall pre- vention alert systems, and AI-driven interactive learning platforms, virtual simulation environments, and clinical case training systems for nurse education. Together, these tools create a practical context in which new nurses can apply AI literacy and develop their professional competencies. However, in resource-limited healthcare institutions, the application of AI remains relatively restricted, and nurses' exposure to AI is often confined to routine information system operations. Moreover, even within the same hospital, the level of AI application may vary across departments. For instance, high-risk and fast-paced units such as emergency departments and intensive care units are more likely to adopt AI-based early warning and support tools earlier, whereas general wards may rely on more basic applications ([Amin et al., 2026)](#analysis-guangli-lu-software-project-administration-methodology-aydogan-s-kok-ay-ergezen-fd-bozkurt-sa-2026-the-effect-of-role-playing-and-zhengyi-ma-investigation-formal-analysis-data-curation-juntong-ai-based-learning-on-nursing-students-knowledge-of-the-nursing-process-and). Therefore, in promoting AI literacy among new nurses, it is essential to consider the specific context in which they work and to develop tiered training programs tailored to the technological conditions of different de- partments. In departments with more advanced AI applications, new nurses can be encouraged to learn through hands-on use of AI tools and engage in experience-sharing with colleagues from other units. In contrast, for departments with more limited AI integration, AI-driven simulation platforms and blended teaching approaches can be used to help new nurses understand the potential of AI in near-realistic sce- narios, thereby strengthening their technological adaptability ([Chen, 2026)](#analysis-guangli-lu-software-project-administration-methodology-aydogan-s-kok-ay-ergezen-fd-bozkurt-sa-2026-the-effect-of-role-playing-and-zhengyi-ma-investigation-formal-analysis-data-curation-juntong-ai-based-learning-on-nursing-students-knowledge-of-the-nursing-process-and). At the institutional level, hospitals should promote interopera- bility and data sharing among AI systems to reduce information silos and create a more efficient intelligent working environment, enabling nurses to effectively leverage AI tools to improve care quality and work effi- ciency ([Fang et al., 2025;](#analysis-guangli-lu-software-project-administration-methodology-aydogan-s-kok-ay-ergezen-fd-bozkurt-sa-2026-the-effect-of-role-playing-and-zhengyi-ma-investigation-formal-analysis-data-curation-juntong-ai-based-learning-on-nursing-students-knowledge-of-the-nursing-process-and) [Harmon et al., 2021)](#analysis-guangli-lu-software-project-administration-methodology-aydogan-s-kok-ay-ergezen-fd-bozkurt-sa-2026-the-effect-of-role-playing-and-zhengyi-ma-investigation-formal-analysis-data-curation-juntong-ai-based-learning-on-nursing-students-knowledge-of-the-nursing-process-and).

At the same time, attention should be paid to the challenges and psychological pressures that new nurses may face when applying AI technologies, including tendencies toward avoidance or resistance. Such negative attitudes often stem from distrust in AI technologies, anxiety about job replacement, and concerns about potential risks ([Baraka et al., 2025;](#analysis-guangli-lu-software-project-administration-methodology-aydogan-s-kok-ay-ergezen-fd-bozkurt-sa-2026-the-effect-of-role-playing-and-zhengyi-ma-investigation-formal-analysis-data-curation-juntong-ai-based-learning-on-nursing-students-knowledge-of-the-nursing-process-and) [Chu et al., 2026)](#analysis-guangli-lu-software-project-administration-methodology-aydogan-s-kok-ay-ergezen-fd-bozkurt-sa-2026-the-effect-of-role-playing-and-zhengyi-ma-investigation-formal-analysis-data-curation-juntong-ai-based-learning-on-nursing-students-knowledge-of-the-nursing-process-and). Nursing educators can address these concerns through experience sharing, helping new nurses understand the sup- portive role and practical value of AI in patient care. Establishing AI mentoring or support groups can also provide timely technical assis- tance, enhance confidence in using technology, and encourage active acceptance and adaptation to AI technologies ([Fan et al., 2025)](#analysis-guangli-lu-software-project-administration-methodology-aydogan-s-kok-ay-ergezen-fd-bozkurt-sa-2026-the-effect-of-role-playing-and-zhengyi-ma-investigation-formal-analysis-data-curation-juntong-ai-based-learning-on-nursing-students-knowledge-of-the-nursing-process-and). Furthermore, nursing educators should not limit their efforts to teaching new nurses how to use AI tools at an operational level. Instead, they should guide them in developing a proactive awareness and capability for job crafting supported by technology. Efforts should be made to foster an organizational climate that encourages job crafting within safe boundaries and prioritizes patient health, granting nurses appropriate autonomy while providing opportunities for participation in decision-making and professional development. This approach enables new nurses to confidently explore ways to optimize their work practices while ensuring patient safety (Wen and Wang, 2025). For example, new nurses can be invited to participate in evaluating the effectiveness of AI tools, encouraged to offer suggestions based on their clinical judgment, and actively involved in discussions on optimizing departmental nursing workflows. Additionally, through mentorship and the establishment of phased goals, new nurses can be guided to proactively refine their work approaches, with timely positive feedback provided to sustain their motivation for learning and career growth.

Globally, new nurses are a key determinant of future nursing quality, and their career growth is closely related to the long-term development potential of the nursing profession (Wise et al., 2023). With the rapid advancement of AI and its deep integration into clinical nursing prac- tice, the findings of this study have broad international relevance. 

Regardless of national or cultural context, insufficient AI literacy may constitute a potential barrier to career growth among new nurses. Given their strong learning ability, adaptability, and high acceptance of new technologies, new nurses are well positioned to translate AI technologies into effective support for clinical practice and to facilitate job crafting ([El-Sayed et al., 2025;](#analysis-guangli-lu-software-project-administration-methodology-aydogan-s-kok-ay-ergezen-fd-bozkurt-sa-2026-the-effect-of-role-playing-and-zhengyi-ma-investigation-formal-analysis-data-curation-juntong-ai-based-learning-on-nursing-students-knowledge-of-the-nursing-process-and) Subasi et al., 2025). Therefore, greater attention should be paid to AI literacy among nurses—particularly new nurses—and to strengthening job crafting capabilities to support higher- quality career growth in the era of AI.

### _5.5._ _Limitations_

This study still has several limitations. First, the intervals and overall duration of data collection were relatively short. Job crafting and career growth typically develop over a longer period as professional experience accumulates. Therefore, this study may not fully capture their long-term developmental trajectories and is better interpreted as reflecting early- stage indicators of career development among new nurses following initial transitional shock. Future research could extend the follow-up period to explore their long-term dynamic evolution and effects. Sec- ond, the core variables relied solely on self-reported data, making them susceptible to common method bias. Although this study employed Harman's single-factor test for diagnosis, this method has limitations, including low statistical power, and cannot fully rule out the presence of common method bias. Future studies may adopt approaches such as incorporating marker variables or matching multi-source data to better address this issue. Third, as the model included autoregressive paths, time-invariant factors were inherently controlled for, and the sample of new nurses exhibited a certain degree of homogeneity. To avoid exces- sive model complexity and potential reductions in estimation stability, not all demographic variables were included as covariates. Therefore, the risk of omitted variable bias remains. However, educational level was included in a sensitivity analysis, which confirmed the robustness of the findings. Future research should incorporate more control variables to provide a more comprehensive and detailed analysis of individual differences. Fourth, the participants were drawn from five tertiary general hospitals across different regions of China. These institutions typically have relatively advanced technological infrastructures and provide greater exposure to AI technologies. Therefore, the findings may not fully represent settings with lower levels of AI integration, which limits the generalizability of the results. Future studies could include healthcare institutions at different levels to compare differences in new nurses' career growth across varying technological environments.

## 6. Conclusion

Using a three-wave longitudinal design, this study comprehensively examined the relationships and dynamic changes among AI literacy, job crafting, and career growth in new nurses and constructed a longitudinal mediation model. The results showed that the mean levels of AI literacy and career growth followed a pattern of initial decline followed by an increase over time, whereas job crafting exhibited a continuous upward trend. AI literacy, job crafting, and career growth were significantly and positively correlated at all time points. AI literacy among new nurses can directly and positively predict their subsequent career growth, with job crafting playing a longitudinal mediating role in this relationship. This study provides new theoretical evidence for developing training strate- gies for new nurses in the era of AI. By enhancing AI literacy and job crafting, it may be possible to promote career growth among new nurses, which is of great significance for the sustainable development of the nursing profession.
